passage:
Counsellor's notes, employee wellbeing desk, 14 March
Noor, 24, came back for a second check-in. Last month she described nights of scrolling until 2 am and feeling flatter afterwards. This time she brought a page from her notebook.
Her plan: phone apps from 8:30 to 9:30 pm, then the phone charges in the kitchen. Each week, one offline thing: a Tuesday walk with a colleague from accounts, a Sunday call with her sister in Srinagar.
She said the first Tuesday walk felt awkward for ten minutes, then easy. 'I still use my phone,' she laughed. 'I just don't use it instead of people.'
She reports sleeping better, and the one walk has become two.
Next: follow-up in a month. I suggested adding a weekend plan only if she wants one.
- Hafsa

qa.q: Where does Noor's phone charge after 9:30 pm?
qa.a: The phone charges in the kitchen.

qa.q: What does Noor's laugh and line 'I just don't use it instead of people' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Noor feels relieved and a little proud, having found a balance rather than giving up the phone altogether.

qa.q: Why does pairing a time window with an offline plan work better than the window alone?
qa.a: The window limits scrolling, while the walk and the call fill that time with real company, so the screen stays a tool rather than a replacement.

qa.q: What might Noor's sister in Srinagar get from the Sunday calls?
qa.a: Her sister likely gets a steady weekly connection and hears Noor's real voice, instead of only seeing posts.

grounding: It shows a young woman setting a window for phone use and pairing it with a weekly walk and call, keeping screens as a tool.

Wednesday, 10:05 pm
Day nine of The Rule: phone apps only between 7 and 8 at night, then airplane mode. I was sure I'd cheat by day three.
I did cheat once, on day four, watching a stranger renovate a flat in another country at midnight. Felt worse after, like always.
The second half of The Rule is the part that actually works: one real plan a week. Last Saturday I walked the lake loop with Aditi. We got lost behind the boat club and laughed so hard a dog barked at us. I didn't check my phone once and didn't miss it.
Tonight at 8 I put the phone down mid-reel. Zainab, you're getting good at this.
Called Aditi instead. We're doing the loop again on Saturday. Bringing better shoes.

qa.q: Where did Zainab and Aditi get lost?
qa.a: They got lost behind the boat club.

qa.q: How did Zainab feel after cheating at midnight on day four?
qa.a: Zainab felt low and regretful afterwards, the same bad feeling late scrolling always brought.

qa.q: Which half of The Rule does Zainab find more useful, and why?
qa.a: The one real plan a week, because the lake walk with Aditi gave laughter and company that scrolling never did.

qa.q: What might Aditi get out of the Saturday walks?
qa.a: Aditi gets a friend who is fully present rather than on a phone, which likely makes the walks fun enough to want to repeat.

grounding: It shows someone limiting phone time to a set hour and pairing it with a weekly walk with a friend, so screens stop replacing company.

passage:
The village school where Asif taught had one bus a day and patchy signal except near the peepal tree. For his first months there, every evening went the same way: he climbed onto the roof of his rented room, where the network was best, and scrolled until midnight, watching friends in Ranchi at cafés and weddings.
One night he realised he hadn't spoken to a single adult except the headmaster in four days.
So he made a rule. Phone on the roof from eight to nine, not after. And one real thing every day: a call to his mother, a chat with the tea-stall owner, carrom with the headmaster's son.
On Sundays he now called Mridul, his college friend, for a proper hour instead of sending him reels. Last week Mridul said, "You sound like yourself again."
Asif still liked his screen. It just wasn't his only company any more.

qa.q: Where did Asif go for the best network?
qa.a: Onto the roof of his rented room.

qa.q: What did Asif feel when he realised he had spoken only to the headmaster in four days?
qa.a: He felt startled and lonely, seeing that scrolling had quietly replaced real company.

qa.q: What makes Asif's rule effective?
qa.a: A fixed hour for the phone plus one real contact every day keeps the screen a tool, not a replacement.

qa.q: How does Mridul experience the change in Asif?
qa.a: Mridul feels happy and relieved, hearing his friend sound like himself again on their Sunday calls.

grounding: A young teacher in a remote village limits his phone to one hour and adds one real contact a day, so screens stop replacing company.

passage:
In her tiny flat in south London, Amara had been spending every evening in bed with her phone, watching strangers cook, travel and fall in love. By the time she looked up it was one in the morning, and she felt emptier than when she'd started.
In January she made a deal with herself. Social apps only between seven and eight, timer on. And every day, one offline thing, even a small one.
Monday she called her grandmother in Lagos. Tuesday she asked Jin, her flatmate, whom she'd barely spoken to in months, if he wanted to cook jollof together. Jin burned the onions; Amara laughed until she cried. Wednesday they walked to the market. Thursday Jin taught her a card game from Busan.
She still watched cooking videos. But now, some nights, she cooked the recipes with someone.

qa.q: When does Amara allow herself social apps?
qa.a: Only between seven and eight, timer on.

qa.q: How did Amara feel at one in the morning before the change?
qa.a: She felt empty and lonely after hours of watching strangers' lives.

qa.q: Why does pairing screen time with an offline plan help?
qa.a: It keeps the phone a tool and adds real contact, like cooking with Jin, that screens can't replace.

qa.q: What might Jin feel when Amara asks to cook together?
qa.a: Jin is probably surprised and pleased, glad to finally connect with a flatmate he barely knew.

grounding: A young woman sets a window for apps and pairs it with a daily offline plan, turning a flatmate into real company.

passage: The staff room at the call centre emptied at the 3 pm break, and Vidya's old habit was to sit alone and scroll until the buzzer. Her phone's weekly report had said five hours a day. Six weeks ago she had made herself a rule, taped inside her locker: "Online 8 to 9 pm only. Plus one real plan a day." Today's plan was on the sticky note: "Walk with Gurleen, 3 pm." Gurleen from the billing team was already at the door with two cutting chais. They walked around the parking lot twice, complaining about a difficult customer and laughing about the new manager's tie. Vidya's phone buzzed in her pocket once. She left it. At nine that night she did open the video site, watched her usual cooking channel for the full hour, and then plugged the phone in across the room.

qa.q: What was written on today's sticky note?
qa.a: It said: Walk with Gurleen, 3 pm.

qa.q: How does Vidya seem to feel on the walk with Gurleen?
qa.a: Vidya seems relaxed and cheerful, laughing about the manager's tie and calm enough to ignore the buzzing phone.

qa.q: Which parts of Vidya's plan make it work?
qa.a: She set a clear online window and paired it with one real plan each day, so the phone stays a tool for her cooking channel, not a replacement for people.

qa.q: How might Gurleen experience these daily walks?
qa.a: Gurleen probably enjoys them too, a chance to vent about customers and share a laugh during a long shift.

grounding: Shows a person setting a fixed window for online time and pairing it with one offline plan each day, so screens stay a tool rather than a substitute for company.
